temperature differences between sheltered valleys and higher 
elevations. With clear skies and light winds promoting strong 
radiational cooling, colder air will settle into the valleys, while

.DISCUSSION /Through Friday/...
Issued at 1110 PM MDT Fri Oct 23 2026

Another day closer to this weekend's storm system, and almost all
of the details regarding precipitation potential remain unclear.

We'll start with what we know. A fairly strong surface cold front
is still on track to arrive Saturday morning, sometime not too
long after sunrise for most of the Denver metro. Unlike many of
our cool season fronts, it will take some time to saturate the low
levels, meaning that low/mid cloud cover will be slow to develop 
in the morning before stratus becomes more widespread during the
afternoon hours. High temperatures Saturday afternoon may only
rebound into the low 50s across most of the lower elevations.

Meanwhile, the main upper level low of interest is spinning over
far southern California tonight, and should track off to the north
and east during the day Saturday. Today's trends have been towards
a slower (further west) and slightly stronger low. As a result,
the deeper plume of moisture also ends up a touch further west.
Most of tonight's CAMs throw a large precipitation shield from
south to north during the afternoon and evening hours, with modest
(~0.05-0.25") amounts as far west as the foothills and as far
north as a Longmont - Greeley line. However, most of the
global/regional deterministic guidance is not nearly as bullish
with this potential, nor are most ensemble members during this
time. It will be worth watching if either of these solutions fold
with the 06/12z guidance later tonight. Of note - some of these
wetter solutions also bring in favorable south-southeasterly flow
into Park County where there could be a few inches of snow 
through Sunday AM.

By Sunday, forecast guidance really likes the idea of spinning up
a well-defined Denver cyclone. As noted in the previous discussion,
temperatures will probably warm up into the upper 50s to low 60s 
where clear skies develop, while many locations along the northern
I-25 corridor and northeastern plains remain socked in stratus 
and see temperatures similar to Saturday. The upper low is 
expected to pivot across the region from Sunday afternoon into 
Monday morning. Again, one notable trend is to have this low be 
stronger/better defined, with a negatively tilted trough axis 
noted by Sunday night. As a result, the surface low over eastern 
Colorado ends up a bit more defined and low-level upslope is a 
touch stronger, while QG ascent is placed over our forecast area. 
Again, guidance is all over the place with the actual track of 
both the upper level and surface features. The ECMWF has been 
relatively consistent placing more substantial QPF over our 
central/northern mountains into the adjacent plains, while many of
this evening's CAMs kept most of the meaningful QPF closer to the
CO/WY border. Our preference here was closer the NBM/ECMWF 
ensemble mean, though I would anticipate more changes to the 
forecast over the next 24-36 hours. At the very least, there's two
well-defined periods for potential rain (and mountain snow) this 
weekend for those looking to see their favorite hydrometeors fall 
out of the sky.

Once the trough lifts to the north of our area Monday, we'll re-

warming trend by Tuesday under a broad warm air advection regime.
Highs most days next week look to be somewhere in the 60s to near

Forecast confidence does decrease pretty quickly next week. Most 
models show a complex (or simply messy) pattern across most of the
western CONUS. The dominant features will be a couple of strong 
shortwaves/closed lows across the Pacific Northwest and the 
northern Great Plains, with a couple weaker shortwaves associated 
with the subtropical jet. The general pattern supports warm and 
dry conditions, though there could be a couple periods of 
cooler/cloudier weather based on the track of those. There are 
signs that the subtropical jet becomes more active by next 
weekend... but it's difficult to translate that into an actual 
forecast at this time. We'll let this current weekend pass by 
before worrying too much about it.

.SHORT TERM (TDY-MON)...24/340 AM.

Fairly benign stretch of weather ahead in the short-term. A 
clearing and drying trend will continue this weekend as gradients 
shift to weakly offshore. Expect the strongest northeast flow to 
occur today. These weak offshore winds will most likely peak below
Advisory levels, with gusts of 20 to 40 mph common in the wind 
prone mountains and valleys. Temperatures will rise 8 to 15 
degrees today compared to the last couple of days. Highs in the 
70s to lower 80s are expected, with an additional few degrees of 
warming on Sunday. After that, little change in temperatures 
expected through at least Monday.

.LONG TERM (TUE-FRI)...24/341 AM.

Northwest to northeast winds will increase Monday Night into
Tuesday, then weaken into Wednesday. This will keep temperatures
largely unchanged with highs in the 70s to lower 80s most common
which is right around normal for this time of the year. 

The pattern will start to change around Thursday, with onshore
flow returning, temperatures dropping, and low pressure forming
over the West Coast. This will open the storm window over
California, with a growing chance of a significant storm impacting
the local area as early as Friday but more so for the weekend. 
There is a 90+% chance for rain sometime in the Oct 30 through Nov
2 timeframe, likely lasting several hours. Halloween activities
are likely to be impacted. There remains a range of outcomes in 
terms of rain amounts, rates, and winds. At this point, the most 
likely outcome is for a moderate- level storm in terms of strength
and impacts, with a low but present risk for a higher level 
storm.

&&

Steep seas near 10 feet will continue through early this morning
for the outer waters. 15-20 knot North winds are likely nearshore
this morning around Malibu, and West winds over many nearshore 
waters in the afternoon hours. Otherwise, high confidence in quiet
conditions this weekend. Northwest winds will increase next week.
SCA conditions are likely Monday and Tuesday for the waters from 
the Central Coast through San Nicolas Island.

Very high tides between 7.5 and 8.0 feet (roughly 1.0-1.5 feet 
above astronomical predictions) are expected during the morning 
hours of Sunday through Thursday over all coastal areas, with the
highest towards Los Angeles County. Monday through Wednesday could
produce the highest on record (current record at San Pedro is 7.93
feet set on Jan 10, 2005 with records going back to 1924).

Minor coastal flooding is likely purely based on the high tides.
While these tides might be the highest of all-time, similar
extreme tides in the past tell us that coastal communities should
expect shallow flooding of harbor walkways, beach parking lots and
bike paths. With swells and surf on the lower-end during these 
extreme tides (2-3 feet), the threat of more significance/damaging
impacts should be limited to the most vulnerable areas that have 
little-to-no sandy beach left and have already seen water damage.

With that said, these is a small change for more elevated surf on
south-facing shores around Wednesday as waves from a southern
Hemisphere storm arrive. The majority of computer projections keep
this wave energy on the small side, but a couple are a little
larger. 

With all of these considerations in play, Coastal Flood 
Advisories are in effect Sunday through Thursday. There is a low 
potential for targeted Coastal Flooding Warnings if a larger swell
develops and produces elevated surf on top of the very high 
tides.

.DISCUSSION...through Halloween.

Water vapor imagery shows a trough overhead with a vort max over 
southern CA in the process of pinching off into a closed low. Behind 
the shortwave, gusty north winds are currently pushing through the 
southern Great Basin and into the northern Mojave Desert. These will 
continue advance southward, encompassing most of the CWA by sunrise. 
Strongest winds anticipated in Death Valley and the southern Owens 
Valley where gusts of 40-50 mph are possible through the morning 
hours. Elsewhere, expecting gusts generally 20-35 mph, weakening 
during the 2nd half of the day. The formation of the closed low will 
cause the system to slowly exit the region, lingering over 
northwestern AZ this afternoon. The cold air aloft, residual 
moisture, and daytime heating should drive isolated to scattered 
showers and maybe even a few storms over eastern Mohave County (20-
40%), with lower chances (10-20%) over southeastern NV and the 
Colorado River Valley. Can't completely rule out an isolated 
instance of flash flooding in eastern Mohave County, but odds are 5% 
at best.

Our low finally exits on Sunday, leaving us in a zonal pattern for a 
few days before transitioning to southwesterly flow later in the 
week. From Sunday - Thursday, the forecast calls for seasonable 
temperatures, light breezes, and dry conditions. Late in the week, 
ensemble guidance shows an energized subtropical jet trying to push 
moisture into the southwestern US. Cluster analysis shows several 
variations of offshore troughing during this time, so there remains 
a fair amount of uncertainty, but there appears to be a good signal 
for the existence of an offshore trough and southwesterly flow over 
us. Should this come to fruition, we should see an increase in 
southwest winds and low to moderate (10-50%) precipitation chances 
around Halloween weekend.

.SHORT TERM...
(Today through Sunday)
Issued at 307 AM EDT Sat Oct 24 2026

South Florida finds itself at the base of a positively tilted mid-level
longwave trough. Water vapor imagery and upper air sounding 
observations from around the state indicate that deep layer dry 
air is currently in place across most of Florida, keeping 
conditions more dry and stable through the region. As the main 
trough axis swings across the state through tomorrow, unsettled 
weather will remain across the more unstable Gulf Stream waters. 
A few isolated showers may hug the Atlantic coastline during the
day, but most activity will remain offshore. Deeper moisture 
remains further southeast over the Bahamas and closer to a 
stalled boundary near eastern Cuba, where a complex of 
thunderstorms is currently ongoing. However, here in South 
Florida, model soundings seem to indicate that moisture content 
will actually trend drier on Saturday. Precipitable water values 
will drop from a near average 1.6 inches, to a bottom tenth 
percentile of 0.8 to 0.9 inches. Models hint at the drier air 
reaching the surface this time, with dewpoints dropping into the 
lower 60s through the middle of the day. As a result, PoPs will be
very low across most of South Florida, less than 10% for most 
areas. In addition to the dry air, subsidence aloft should keep 
any showers from being able to mature or develop. Coastal 
convergence may be possible, but there is very low confidence for
rain amounts to be anything greater than half an inch through 
tomorrow afternoon.

Forecast confidence for the Saturday night through Sunday period has 
quite honestly decreased. Ensemble and deterministic guidance 
continues to struggle with a solution for the shortwave feature 
coming off of the Carolina coast. There is less agreement among 
guidance as to weather this feature develops into a closed mid-level 
low as it tracks southward along the Florida coastline, or 
whether it stays an open wave and join the overall longwave 
troughing pattern. Solutions also differ as to how fast and how 
far east and south this feature will move over the next two days. 
This has major implications on the amount of rainfall South 
Florida may get. A deeper, slower, and more westerly tracking 
system would increase chances of precipitation areawide. However, 
most model guidance has continued to trend lower with 
precipitation amounts. WPC QPF ensemble clusters show that 1 to 
1.5 inches through Monday would be the highest confidence scenario
to play out. Yet, there is one cluster of solutions that shows a 
scenario of 3 to 4 inches possible (but this is a lower 
confidence scenario). Overall, better dynamics aloft and increased
streams of vorticity across the region will favor greater shower 
and storm activity. PoPs will climb into the 70% to 80% range over
the eastern metro. Coastal convergence may allow for several 
storms to focus along the coastline for several hours, so a Slight
Risk of excessive rainfall exits for minor urban flooding along 
low lying and poor drainage locations. 

Breezy northeasterly winds will continue to strengthen through the 
weekend for all areas. Breezy winds may combine with high surf and 
unusually high tides over the weekend. This may result in 
moderate to potentially major tidal flooding for coastal areas 
along Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties. Remember to never 
drive, walk, or wade across flooded roads. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through Friday)
Issued at 307 AM EDT Sat Oct 24 2026

By the time Sunday night rolls around, strong surface high pressure 
over the mid-Atlantic states and deepening surface troughing over 
the northern Caribbean will create a tightening pressure gradient 
across the Florida coastline. As a result, winds will continue to 
strengthen into Monday and Tuesday. Sustained winds over the waters 
will already be howling at 30 mph starting on Sunday, but the 
strongest overall winds inland look to be moreso on Monday. Some 
areas will be flirting with Wind Advisory criteria, with gusts of 
35 to 40 mph possible. There is pretty high confidence that winds 
will at least reach 25 mph for many locations, but probabilities 
for winds greater than 30 mph area only around 30%. Nevertheless, 
these conditions have the potential to break weak tree branches 
and blow around loose objects and debris.

Strong winds and high surf will combine with the highest King Tides 
of the year early next week. This will result in the potential for 
moderate and major tidal flooding. This tidal flooding may also be 
exacerbated by coastal showers and rainfall, which could lead to 
significant water rises along the far eastern metro areas. While the 
peak tides will be during the beginning of the week, moderate coastal 
flooding may persist through the end of the week as we come out of 
this full moon phase.

Deeper moisture, with increased PWATs of around 1.6 to 1.8 inches, 
will persist over South Florida through at least Tuesday. This will 
keep the potential of scattered showers and storms moving along the 
eastern half of South Florida. A few localized stronger storms and 
coastal convergence may create some minor urban flooding concerns. 
However, the threat of rainfall will generally be on the downtrend 
after Monday as the mid-level troughing pattern finally ejects 
out into the Atlantic. Ridging from the Gulf and drier air from 
the north will begin to exert more influence over Florida for the 
middle to end of the week. This will likely result in decreasing 
coverage of showers and storms areawide. But with persistent 
northeast flow continuing, pesky onshore showers from the Gulf 
Stream will continue to be a nuisance each day through the end of
the week.

&&

.AVIATION...
(12Z TAFS)
Issued at 726 AM EDT Sat Oct 24 2026

Mainly VFR conditions will prevail across South Florida

.MARINE...

Hazardous marine conditions will continue through the

the latter half of the weekend. Northeasterly winds will increase 
into the 20 to 25 kt range for both the Atlantic and Gulf waters on

A high risk of rip currents will persist for all Atlantic beaches 
through at least the middle of next week. Surf heights will begin to 
climb today but peak on Sunday and Monday. Dangerous surf heights of

Atlantic coast. See the hydrology section below for a discussion on

middle of the week.

The combination of elevated coastal water levels due to King

area that can easily become saturated due to antecedent rainfalls

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 250 AM CDT Sat Oct 24 2026

Slow-moving band of rain showers is exiting eastward across western 
WI, with a more recent batch trailing showers captured on radar over 
portions of central MN. These showers have developed within a 40-
50kt LLJ that spans from SW to NE across MN. Not anticipating these 
showers to be too heavy as latest ACARS data along with forecast 
soundings depict a very dry lowest 10k feet of the column along 
with a lack of elevated instability. Breezy southeasterly surface 
flow combined with cloud cover is working to limit cooling, so 
morning lows are on track to only dip into the upper 50s to lower 
60s (this is ~5-7 degrees warmer than normal highs this late in 
October!). 

One more warm day ahead, as the Upper Midwest begins the day 
located within the warm sector of a deepening surface cyclone 
positioned over south central Canada. The system is progged to 
rapidly lift northeast through the day and will send a trailing 
cold front southeastward across the forecast area. The front is 
progged to be near the border of the Dakotas and MN by daybreak,
where showers and a few rumbles of thunder will be possible through
the morning. The morning frontal position sets the stage for a 
10+ degree high temperature gradient from western MN to western
WI. The earlier frontal passage across western MN will limit 
heating and support highs in the lower 60s. Surface heating is 
forecast to be more efficient through the morning and into the 
early afternoon to the east of the front over much of east- 
central and southeastern MN as well as western WI. Filtered 
sunshine and ongoing WAA will yield highs in the low to mid 70s 
for locations that remain east of the front through midday. The

half of the forecast area) will arrive early in the work week as a

* The next significant chance for widespread rainfall is not

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 211 AM EDT Sat Oct 24 2026

This Morning through the Weekend...

It is another clear and calm morning across the region as the 
influence of broad sfc high pressure and upper level ridging 
continues to bring quiescent weather across much of the eastern 
CONUS. Typical ridge-valley and urban-rural differences in 
temperatures are observed, with readings ranging from the upper 30s 
to the low 50s at this hour. The main thing we're watching through 
mid morning will be the development of patchy fog in valleys and 
near bodies of water where dewpoint depressions will be lowest. 
Patchy frost also can't be ruled out in the coldest spots; however, 
coverage should be limited so no headlines are anticipated.

Outside of patchy valley fog development, no significant weather is 
expected this weekend. Pleasant fall weather is expected to continue 
as high pressure east of the Appalachians and upper ridging over the 
Mississippi Valley continue to exert their influence, bringing mild 
and dry conditions to central KY and southern IN. As the upper ridge 
gets nudged slightly eastward through the weekend, marginal rises in 
1000-850 mb thicknesses should support temperatures trending a 
degree or so above persistence each day, with highs generally in the 
low-to-mid 70s. Large diurnal temperature swings should also 
continue, with temps dropping into the 40s in most areas each night.

Next Week through the end of October...

Blocking high pressure over the Gulf of Alaska will keep mean 
synoptic-scale troughing over the western CONUS through early next 
week, with upper ridging and sfc high pressure continuing to support 
dry weather across the region. A few shortwave disturbances may try 
to eject along the top of the eastern US ridge; however, they should 
be fairly moisture-starved and would be expected to bring little 
more than a few extra clouds during the mid-week period. As a 
result, dry weather is expected to persist through all of next week, 
with recent global model guidance trending downward for rain chances 
late next week. Temperatures should be relatively consistent from 
day-to-day next week, and should be above average overall.

This extended stretch of rain-free weather will lead to increasing 
precipitation deficits for both the month of October and 
meteorological fall (since Sep 1st). Worsening drought conditions 
are likely where they currently exist, and the spatial extent of 
drought will likely increase over the coming 7-10 days.

The next chance of rain on the horizon arrives Halloween weekend, 
though only about 20% of GEFS/EPS solutions show rain on Halloween. 
Better chances for rain should hold off until the first few days of 
November, when a stronger system may move across the Ohio Valley 
(forecast confidence medium, stay tuned for more details next week).

Issued 1030 PM CDT Fri Oct 23 2026

Tonight through Saturday night:

Light southeasterly winds and lingering humidity over Lake MI 
have formed a bank of fog and low stratus clouds drifting into 
Sheboygan county and points north. METARS and DOT cameras 
confirm the fog is dense in Sheboygan County, and a Dense Fog 
Advisory will remain in effect through 9 AM Saturday morning 
(unless trends warrant a change). An expansion of this Advisory 
southward into Washington and Ozaukee counties later tonight is 
possible, given GOES Night Fog RGB composites and surface 
observations are beginning to indicate a southward creep to the
fog over time, mainly along and east of the Kettle Moraine 
hills. We could even see this fog continue south into the MKE 
metro late tonight, though forecast confidence is low. 

The combination of continued airflow at the surface, abundant 
high- altitude cloud cover, and weak terrain-locking of the 
Kettle Moraine hills should prevent any fog formation further 
inland. From a Fond du Lac to Walworth line westward, looking
fog free for tonight at this time. 

Into post-dawn Saturday morning, winds turn due south and
accelerate slightly, clearing away any lingering fog. Additional
periods of broken high-altitude cloud cover are anticipated 
through Saturday and Saturday night, but dry weather continues 
all the same. Highs in the low 70s expected inland; some 
shoreline ventilation (SSE winds) could hold highs to the mid 
60s for far eastern WI.

Sheppard

&&

.LONG TERM...
Issued 1030 PM CDT Fri Oct 23 2026

Sunday through Friday:

Low pressure tracking east across Hudson Bay Canada this weekend 
will drag a cold front into WI. The front should reach
northwestern portions of WI by late Saturday night into Sunday
morning, with strong high pressure over Saskatchewan then
forcing the front across southern WI later Sunday through Sunday
night. Predominantly dry weather is expected to accompany the
frontal passage, and the late arrival of the front allows
daytime highs to reach the low 70s Sunday. CAA behind the front
kicks in late Sunday night into Monday, with northeasterly 
winds off the lake. As such, central and eastern WI are forecast
to observe highs in the 50s, with highs in the mid 60s further
west along the southern edge of the state. 

Meanwhile on Monday, a 500mb shortwave trough will dig into the
central Great Plains, phasing with the aforementioned frontal 
boundary to seed surface low pressure. This low pressure looks 
to lift northeast into Monday night, bringing some 5-15% rain 
chances to the CWA. The bulk of the QPF and higher precip 
chances with this system land in MN and northwestern WI, 
leaving us predominantly dry as it passes. The remnant 
baroclinic zone from that activity then sets the stage for an 
additional upper trough and surface low to slide northeast from 
the Plains midweek. The placement of precip with this second 
system is less certain, but could track through the same 
corridor of MN / NW-WI or further east. ~15-30% precip chances 
are forecast for the CWA Wednesday until ensembles converge on a
system track. In any scenario, we will be in the warm sector of
both passing systems, resulting in a warming trend towards
midweek. 

This same pattern looks to continue later this week, with
additional rain chances. 

Sheppard

&&

Issued 1030 PM CDT Fri Oct 23 2026

Open Waters / Synopsis:
High pressure around 30.4 inches will sag south from Quebec into
the northeastern CONUS overnight into Saturday morning. 
Meanwhile, 29.4 inch low pressure tracks from northeast Montana
into Manitoba. Positioning of these surface features is resulting
in generally south to southeasterly winds across the waters. Areas
of fog, some of which have been dense, will likely continue
through the overnight hours over the northern two thirds of the
lake, gradually dissipating post-dawn Saturday morning as winds 
turn due south and accelerate. That being said, satellite
signatures and ship observations currently confirm that the worst
of the fog is in the eastern and western nearshore zones, rather
than the open waters. 

The aforementioned area of low pressure will continue on toward 
the Hudson Bay by Saturday evening as it deepens to near 29.2 
inches. Progression of the low will maintain generally southerly 
flow across the waters, with gusts between 25-30 knots possible 
over the northern half of the lake Saturday afternoon and night. 
Can't rule out an isolated gust approaching gale force during this
time frame, with conditions not expected to be widespread enough 
for headlines.

Winds will trend southwesterly while steadily weakening ahead of an 
approaching cold front on Sunday. Currently expecting the front to 
move south across Lake Michigan late Sunday afternoon into Sunday 
evening, bringing a breezy northeast wind shift. Gales are not 
anticipated during the frontal passage, with any isolated rain 
showers expected to remain over the far northern part of the lake. 
Breezy northeast winds will continue through Monday as 30.7 inch 
high pressure slides into Ontario from the Canadian Great Plains. 
Winds will trend easterly and eventually southerly Tuesday into 
the middle of next week as the aforementioned high shifts into the
northeastern United States. Widespread rain chances return 
Wednesday into Friday.

Nearshore Zones:
A Small Craft Advisory is in effect north of Port Washington
from Noon to 10 PM Saturday. Accelerating southerly winds 
expected Saturday, obtaining gusts to roughly 20-25 kt by midday
and leading to gradually building waves. Sig Wave Heights crest
between 3 and 5 feet Saturday afternoon, and linger into the 
evening as winds subside. 

Additional Advisory conditions are looking likely Monday into
Tuesday, with gusty northeast winds and building waves expected
behind a cold front.

.PREV DISCUSSION...
Issued at 336 PM EDT Wed Oct 7 2026

DISCUSSION...

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as 
the energetic jet stream resides mostly across Canada. Stacked low 
centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations. 

Brief but strong warm up on Saturday as strong ridging over the 
Plains advances eastward over the Great Lakes. ECMWF is a touch 
warmer (~18C at 850mb) than GFS (-16C) Saturday with strong 
southwesterly flow into the region. Current forecast is for temps to 
touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later. 

This warmup will be brief as attention the turns to TS Isaias which 
is set to make landfall over MS Friday evening then getting drawn 
northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

MARINE...

Moderate southwesterly winds gradually weaken this evening as a cold 
front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass, 
and given the rejuvenated low-level jet winds, mixing likely 
delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around 
30 knots over portions of Lake Huron Thursday afternoon, with 
marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft 
Advisory may be needed over The Thumb should confidence rise in the 
frequency of 25+ knot gusts, but any higher end gusts further north 
should be infrequent enough to preclude a Gale Warning. Mid/Upper 
Mississippi Valley high pressure then expands into the area Thursday 
night and Friday offering weaker winds with a southerly shift.

.FORECAST UPDATE...
Issued at 914 AM EDT Sat Oct 24 2026

Surface analysis this morning shows strong high pressure centered 
over NY and the upper St. Lawrence river valley. This large high was 
extending its influence west across Indiana to easterm TX and 
Eastern OK. A frontal boundary was found over the eastern Dakotas 
and the High plains. Skies were mostly clear across Indiana, but 
GOES16 did show a few high clouds within the Wabash Valley. Water 
Vapor showed strong ridging still in place aloft over the 
Mississippi Valley and western Grerat Lakes, but a tropical plume of 
moisture was noted on the back side of the ridge, streaming north 
across the high plains. 

The large high pressure system and ridging aloft to the west of 
Indiana will continue to provide subsidence and mostly sunny skies 
today. Forecast soundings through the day suggest a dry column as we 
have seen over the past several days. Some high cloud will continue 
to persist within the Wabash valley, but all in all, Mostly Sunny 
will be the rule. Looks for highs near persistence, in the lower 
70s. Overall, ongoing forecast remains in good shape.

&&

.DISCUSSION (Today through Friday)...
Issued at 210 AM EDT Sat Oct 24 2026

Quiet weather with above normal temperatures will continue through 
much of next week, with rain chances returning around Halloween.

Early This Morning through Sunday...

Subsidence from upper ridging and surface high pressure will 
continue to provide dry conditions through Sunday. Winds will remain 
light. High clouds will spill across the ridge into the area at 
times.

Look for highs around 70 to the lower 70s today and in the lower to 
middle 70s Sunday. Lows will be in the 40s (did cut guidance for 
lows tonight in favored cold areas given what has happened recently).

Monday through Wednesday...

An upper trough across southern Canada will help suppress the upper 
ridge south on Monday, which will allow a surface cold front 
to sag into central Indiana on Monday. The front won't get much 
farther south as upper flow will become near parallel to it. 
Generally only high level moisture will be available, and upper 
support is nowhere nearby. Thus, dry conditions will persist.

Additional upper waves moving through the flow, mainly to the 
northwest of the area, will bring the front back north and out of 
the area Tuesday into Wednesday. Again, little to no local forcing 
and no moisture will keep the area dry.

Highs will be in the lower to middle 70s Monday and Wednesday. 
Behind the front on Tuesday, highs will be around 70 to the lower 
70s.

Thursday onward...

Weak upper ridging will linger into Friday, keeping a front to the 
northwest and continuing the dry conditions with above normal 
temperatures.

Uncertainty increases for Halloween as a broad upper trough begins 
to slowly approach the area. Some guidance has showers in the area 
on Halloween while others keep them west until later Saturday night. 
Will stick with blended guidance's chance PoPs but with low 
confidence. Temperatures look to remain above normal.

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 255 AM CDT Sat Oct 24 2026

A high pressure ridge is dominating the eastern half of the country 
with a cutoff low moving through the desert southwest. This high 
pressure is bringing height rises and clear skies to the Ozarks with 
a light southeasterly wind. A slight increase in upper-level 
moisture will result in increased cloud cover throughout the day 
today, but there will still be plenty of clearing for highs to reach 
the upper 70s (and low 80s for some). Southerly flow will add a WAA 
component, also contributing to the highs 10+ degrees above normal 
for late October. Lows will also be warm (climatologically
speaking), especially with cloud cover increasing tonight -- 
generally in the upper 40s in south- central Missouri up to the 
mid-50s in SW MO/SE KS. Sunday will largely be a repeat of today
with slightly more cloud cover.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 255 AM CDT Sat Oct 24 2026

To start the workweek, shortwave energy ejecting out of the 
southwest will result in very minor height falls that act to 
decrease our highs by a few degrees, putting them closer to the mid-
70s. Moisture will be too meager for any meaningful precipitation 
chances, though the NBM puts a small pocket of 20% PoPs in eastern 
Kansas Monday night. All in all, the impact of the shortwave will be 
minor, and we will be back to regularly scheduled highs in the upper 
70s by Wednesday.

Global models essentially depict the low pressure system currently 
in the desert southwest lifting sharply northwest of Missouri over 
the course of the week and impacting the southern Plains and Midwest 
very little. After the shortwave moves out Wednesday, we return to a 
zonal/slightly ridged pattern until potentially late week as some 
disorganized shortwave energy trails in the wake of the more 
dominant troughing that lifted to the north. Models begin to diverge 
quite a bit on this scenario at this lead time, and while this could 
be the next most probable rain maker for the area over Halloweekend, 
there is little certainty at this time. If it pans out, we could 
also see a slight decrease in temperatures in addition to rain, but 
such a weak synoptic feature likely wouldn't lower highs by much. 
The NBM currently buys in to the precipitation scenario, and has an 
interquartile range for highs on Halloween between 67 and 75 for 
Springfield (63 being the normal high). We will be watching this
feature closely as models are able to better resolve it with
shorter lead time.

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 228 AM CDT Sat Oct 24 2026

A slow moving upper-level ridge remains over the central CONUS 
keeping dry and seasonably warm conditions in the Mid-Mississippi 
Valley through the weekend and into Monday. As a result, very little 
change in the weather day-to-day is expected. The only change is the 
presence of some upper-level clouds. The stubborn ridge continues to 
drive high temperatures into the mid to upper 70s, with some areas 
possibly exceeding 80 on Sunday depending on the thickness of the 
clouds. Dry air will allow for radiative cooling overnight keeping 
low temperatures in the upper 40s to low 50s, with the 40s 
predominately being in the river valleys and southeastern MO and 
southwestern IL. This is due to the presence of fewer clouds in that 
region, which will allow for more efficient radiative cooling 
overnight.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY NIGHT THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 228 AM CDT Sat Oct 24 2026

Over the western CONUS, a deep upper-level trough is present and is 
expected to propagate to the northeast toward the north-central 
CONUS and into the Midwest during the middle of the week. Guidance 
is in good consensus that as the trough tracks northeast it will 
reduce the amplitude of the ridge over the region. The current 
forecasted track of the trough will cause the associated cold front 
to stay well to the north of the region, resulting in dry and 
seasonably warm conditions in the region continuing through the 
entire week. High temperatures will remain in the 70s each day. 

Earlier guidance had indicated a potential pattern change at the end 
of the week, but latest model trends indicate stronger confidence 
that the ridge remains in place through the end of the week. 
Yesterday, the NBM and LREF guidances continued to hint at the 
possibility of a cold front coming at the end of the week with IQRs 
of 10-15 degrees for Thursday and Friday, but latest runs have IQRs 
of 5-10 degrees by raising the 25th percentile from being in the 60s 
to being in the low 70s. At the same time, this model trend has also 
decreased the chance of rain at the end of the week down to 10-30 
percent on Friday while increasing the chances the following weekend 
ahead of the potential cold front.
